Adult females of the Kori salamander Hynobius yangi ultimately attain a snout–vent length of 6.14 cm [Li = 6.14 cm], whereas males reach a slightly larger ultimate SVL of 6.26 cm [Li = 6.26 cm]. This modest degree of sexual size dimorphism, with males being marginally larger, is noteworthy among hynobiids and may relate to male–male competition for access to breeding sites under the coarse woody debris of montane streams. Females become reproductively mature upon reaching a snout–vent length of 5.5 cm [Lp = 5.5 cm], while males achieve puberty at a smaller size of 5 cm [Lp = 5 cm]. Such sex-specific maturation thresholds likely reflect the different energetic demands imposed by egg production versus sperm competition, a pattern observed across several congeners.

Neonates emerge weighing just 0.0111 grams [Wwb = 0.0111 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of approximately 2.77 millimeters observed in field-laid gelatinous egg masses. This minute birth mass represents a substantial maternal investment given that clutches typically contain many small, yolk-rich ova. Throughout larval development at a constant water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis has been recorded as 90 days , a relatively rapid transition compared to other Asian hynobiids that may require several months of aquatic growth. The period immediately following yolk-sac larva resorption and the onset of exogenous feeding represents a critical bottleneck, as the tiny endotrophic larva must efficiently capture aquatic microinvertebrates to sustain growth.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 2.5 years [tp = approximately 2.5 years], marking the point at which gonadal maturation and gametogenesis onset are first detectable. This relatively late sexual maturation, equivalent to about 912 days, suggests a slow life-history strategy consistent with the species' montane habitat and cool, stable stream temperatures. The wet weight of a fully grown adult, or ultimate wet weight, is estimated at 2.64 grams [Wwi = 2.64 grams], a projection based on morphological scaling relationships from the related species Onychodactylus japonicus. This modest adult mass, combined with the protracted juvenile period, implies that individuals must accumulate considerable somatic resources before reproductive activation becomes energetically feasible.

Embryonic development in Hynobius yangi proceeds with eggs incubated at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], resulting in an age at birth of 35 days [ab = 35 days]. This incubation period, spanning roughly five weeks, is typical for hynobiid salamanders breeding in cool headwater streams and reflects the temperate thermal regime of the Korean Peninsula. Upon hatching, the aquatic larvae rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to filter feeding on suspended organic particles and small invertebrates. The maximum lifespan observed in captive individuals under similar thermal conditions reaches 11 years [am = 11 years], an impressive longevity for an amphibian of this diminutive size and one that suggests a life cycle characterized by delayed reproduction and extended adult survival at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. The interplay between the prolonged juvenile stage and extended adult lifespan underscores a demographic strategy adapted to environments with low but stable resource availability, where annual survival rates are high enough to compensate for delayed reproductive onset.

Reproductive output under optimal thermal conditions has been documented at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], where females produce 66 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 66 eggs per clutch] and can deposit up to 3 clutches per year [F_R_i = up to 3 clutches per year]. This maximum reproduction rate, combining high fecundity with relatively frequent nesting bouts, allows the species to offset high rates of early-life mortality common in lentic-breeding amphibians. The warmer 26 °C conditions accelerate ovarian recrudescence and shorten inter-clutch intervals, whereas cooler stream temperatures typical of their natural habitat likely reduce annual clutch frequency. Such thermal sensitivity of reproductive scheduling underscores the vulnerability of Hynobius yangi to climate-driven shifts in montane stream thermal regimes, as even modest increases in mean water temperature could disrupt the delicate phenological synchrony between larval emergence and peak prey abundance.
